## Objectives

By the end of today, you will be able to:

1. Define the autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation functions
1. Explain how the spectrum relates to the autocorrelation function
1. Identify red noise, white noise, and a periodic component from a spectrum
1. Read a spectrogram

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
using CairoMakie,
    CSV, DataFrames, Dates, DSP, LaTeXStrings, Printf, Random, Statistics, StatsBase
set_theme!(theme_minimal(); fontsize=20)
colors = Makie.wong_colors()
Random.seed!(543)
```

# Autocorrelation

## Definition

The **autocorrelation at lag $h$** is the correlation between $X_t$ and $X_{t-h}$:

$$
\rho_h = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X_t,\, X_{t-h})}{\mathrm{Var}(X_t)}
$$

Assuming stationarity, $\rho_h$ depends on $h$ alone.

$\rho_0 = 1$, and $\rho_h \in [-1, 1]$.

## The AR(1) model

$$
x_t = a\,x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2), \qquad |a| < 1
$$

The autocorrelation is

$$
\rho_h = a^{|h|}
$$

## How the decay depends on $a$

```{julia}
#| echo: false
lags = 0:30
fig = Figure(; size=(900, 330))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{lag } h", ylabel=L"\rho_h")
for (i, a) in enumerate([0.3, 0.7, 0.95])
    lines!(ax, collect(lags), a .^ lags; linewidth=3, color=colors[i], label=L"a = %$(a)")
    scatter!(ax, collect(lags), a .^ lags; markersize=7, color=colors[i])
end
hlines!(ax, [0]; color=:black, linewidth=0.8)
axislegend(ax; position=:rt)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
for a in [0.3, 0.7, 0.95]
    @printf("a = %.2f: rho_10 = %.4f\n", a, a^10)
end
```

## $\sigma$ does not affect the autocorrelation

```{julia}
#| echo: false
function simulate_ar(coefficients, n; sigma=1.0)
    x = zeros(n)
    p = length(coefficients)
    for t in (p + 1):n
        x[t] = sum(coefficients[j] * x[t - j] for j in 1:p) + sigma * randn()
    end
    return x
end

fig = Figure(; size=(900, 330))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"t", ylabel=L"x_t", title="two runs, same a = 0.7")
ax2 = Axis(
    fig[1, 2]; xlabel=L"\text{lag } h", ylabel=L"\hat\rho_h", title="same autocorrelation"
)
for (i, sigma) in enumerate([1.0, 4.0])
    x = simulate_ar([0.7], 20_000; sigma=sigma)
    lines!(ax1, x[1:120]; linewidth=1.2, color=colors[i], label=L"\sigma = %$(sigma)")
    scatter!(ax2, collect(lags), autocor(x, lags); markersize=8, color=colors[i])
end
lines!(ax2, collect(lags), 0.7 .^ lags; linewidth=2, color=:black, linestyle=:dash)
axislegend(ax1; position=:rt)
fig
```

Correlation is scale-free, so $a$ shows up in $\rho_h$; $\sigma$ does not.

## What a short record can tell you

The formula $\rho_h = a^{|h|}$ describes the model.
An estimate $\hat\rho_h$ from $n$ observations is subject to *sampling variability*:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
fig = Figure(; size=(950, 330))
for (i, n_obs) in enumerate([50, 200, 20_000])
    ax = Axis(
        fig[1, i];
        xlabel=L"\text{lag } h",
        ylabel=i == 1 ? L"\hat\rho_h" : "",
        title="n = $(n_obs)",
    )
    x = simulate_ar([0.7], n_obs)
    stem!(ax, collect(0:20), autocor(x, 0:20); color=colors[i])
    lines!(ax, collect(0:20), 0.7 .^ (0:20); linewidth=2, color=:black, linestyle=:dash)
    hlines!(ax, [0]; color=:black, linewidth=0.8)
    ylims!(ax, -0.6, 1.05)
end
fig
```

# Partial autocorrelation

## Definition

An AR(1) has $\rho_2 = a^2 \neq 0$, but $x_{t-2}$ does not appear in the model.
The lag-2 correlation exists because $x_{t-2}$ affects $x_{t-1}$, which affects $x_t$.

The **partial autocorrelation at lag $h$** removes the contribution of intervening lags:

$$
\phi_h = \text{coefficient on } x_{t-h} \text{ in a regression of } x_t \text{ on } x_{t-1}, \ldots, x_{t-h}
$$

## PACF of an AR(1)

$\phi_1 = a$, because regressing $x_t$ on $x_{t-1}$ alone recovers the AR(1) coefficient.

Adding $x_{t-2}$ to the regression adds no predictive power, so $\phi_h = 0$ for $h > 1$.

$$
\phi_1 = a, \qquad \phi_h = 0 \ \text{ for } h > 1
$$

For an AR($p$), $\phi_h = 0$ for $h > p$.

The autocorrelation decays gradually; the partial autocorrelation cuts off, and the cutoff identifies the order.

## AR(1), both diagnostics

```{julia}
#| echo: false
ar1 = simulate_ar([0.7], 20_000)
fig = Figure(; size=(900, 330))
ax1 = Axis(
    fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{lag } h", ylabel=L"\hat\rho_h", title="autocorrelation"
)
stem!(ax1, collect(0:20), autocor(ar1, 0:20); color=colors[1])
lines!(ax1, collect(0:20), 0.7 .^ (0:20); linewidth=2, color=:black, linestyle=:dash)
ax2 = Axis(
    fig[1, 2];
    xlabel=L"\text{lag } h",
    ylabel=L"\hat\phi_h",
    title="partial autocorrelation",
)
stem!(ax2, collect(1:20), pacf(ar1, 1:20); color=colors[2])
for ax in (ax1, ax2)
    hlines!(ax, [0]; color=:black, linewidth=0.8)
    ylims!(ax, -0.4, 1.05)
end
fig
```

# Second order

## What does a second lag buy?

An AR(1) can only decay: today's value drifts back toward zero, and the rate depends on $a$.

Adding a second lag lets the process look back two steps:

$$
x_t = a_1 x_{t-1} + a_2 x_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t
$$

The character of the solution depends on $a_1$ and $a_2$:

- **Decay** (both roots real and inside the unit circle)
- **Oscillation** (complex roots inside the unit circle)
- **Blow up** (a root outside the unit circle, the model is unstable)

The roots of $z^2 - a_1 z - a_2 = 0$ are complex when $a_1^2 + 4a_2 < 0$.

## Our AR(2) example

Take $a_1 = 1.2$, $a_2 = -0.7$.

$$
a_1^2 + 4a_2 = 1.44 - 2.8 = -1.36 < 0
$$

Complex roots, so it oscillates: damped, and never repeating exactly.

## AR(2) partial autocorrelation

$$
\phi_1 = \frac{a_1}{1 - a_2}, \qquad \phi_2 = a_2, \qquad \phi_h = 0 \text{ for } h > 2
$$

For our $a_1 = 1.2$, $a_2 = -0.7$:

```{julia}
#| echo: false
a1, a2 = 1.2, -0.7
@printf("φ₁ = %.3g, φ₂ = %.3g", a1 / (1 - a2), a2)
```

## AR(2), both diagnostics

```{julia}
#| echo: false
ar2 = simulate_ar([1.2, -0.7], 20_000)
fig = Figure(; size=(900, 330))
ax1 = Axis(
    fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{lag } h", ylabel=L"\hat\rho_h", title="autocorrelation"
)
stem!(ax1, collect(0:20), autocor(ar2, 0:20); color=colors[1])
ax2 = Axis(
    fig[1, 2];
    xlabel=L"\text{lag } h",
    ylabel=L"\hat\phi_h",
    title="partial autocorrelation",
)
stem!(ax2, collect(1:20), pacf(ar2, 1:20); color=colors[2])
for ax in (ax1, ax2)
    hlines!(ax, [0]; color=:black, linewidth=0.8)
    ylims!(ax, -0.8, 1.05)
end
fig
```


# The spectrum

## Any time series is a sum of sine waves

A zero-mean time series with $n$ points can be written exactly as

$$
x_t = \sum_{k=1}^{n/2} \left[ A_k \cos(2\pi f_k t) + B_k \sin(2\pi f_k t) \right]
$$

at frequencies $f_k = k/n$.
Each frequency contributes some amplitude; the spectrum measures how much variance each one carries.

## Reconstructing from frequencies

```{julia}
#| echo: false
n_demo = 200
t_demo = 1:n_demo
x_demo = simulate_ar([1.2, -0.7], n_demo)
ft = [sum(x_demo[t] * exp(-2π * im * k * t / n_demo) for t in 1:n_demo) for k in 0:(n_demo ÷ 2)]
amplitudes = abs.(ft) ./ n_demo

fig = Figure(; size=(900, 500))
ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1:2]; ylabel=L"x_t", title="original series")
lines!(ax1, t_demo, x_demo; linewidth=1.2, color=colors[1])
hidexdecorations!(ax1; grid=false)

partial_sums = [3, 10, n_demo ÷ 2]
for (i, K) in enumerate(partial_sums)
    ax = Axis(
        fig[2, i];
        xlabel=L"t",
        ylabel=i == 1 ? L"x_t" : "",
        title="first $K frequencies",
    )
    reconstruction = zeros(n_demo)
    for k in 1:K
        for t in 1:n_demo
            reconstruction[t] +=
                2 * real(ft[k + 1]) / n_demo * cos(2π * k * t / n_demo) -
                2 * imag(ft[k + 1]) / n_demo * sin(2π * k * t / n_demo)
        end
    end
    reconstruction .+= real(ft[1]) / n_demo
    lines!(ax, t_demo, reconstruction; linewidth=1.2, color=colors[i + 1])
    ylims!(ax, extrema(x_demo) .* 1.1)
end
fig
```

Adding more frequencies recovers more of the original signal.
All $n/2$ frequencies recover it exactly.

## Variance by frequency

- The **spectrum** $S(f)$ is the variance of the record at frequency $f$.
- Frequency is in cycles per time step, so $f = 1/12$ is one cycle every 12 steps.
- Frequencies run from 0 to $1/2$ (the Nyquist frequency).

::: {.callout-note title="Wiener-Khinchin theorem"}
The spectrum is the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function:

$$
S(f) = \sum_{h=-\infty}^{\infty} \rho_h \, e^{-2\pi i f h}
$$

For supplementary notes, read @kantz_nonlinear:2004 §2.3, printed pp. 18-23.
:::

## White noise

A **white noise** sequence is a set of independent, identically distributed random variables, each with mean zero and variance $\sigma^2$.

$\rho_h = 0$ for all $h \neq 0$: because the draws are independent, there is no autocorrelation at any lag.

Since $S(f)$ is the Fourier transform of $\rho_h$, and $\rho_h$ is zero everywhere except $h = 0$:

$$
S(f) = \sigma^2 \qquad \text{for every } f
$$

A flat spectrum: equal power at every frequency (by analogy with white light).
Adding white noise to a signal adds the same amount of variance at every frequency.

## AR(1) spectrum: red noise

$$
S(f) = \frac{\sigma^2}{\left|1 - a\,e^{-2\pi i f}\right|^{2}}
    = \frac{\sigma^2}{1 - 2a\cos 2\pi f + a^{2}}
$$

At $f = 0$: denominator is $(1-a)^2$, power is largest.
At $f = 1/2$: denominator is $(1+a)^2$, power is smallest.

For $a > 0$, power decreases with frequency.
Called **red noise** because red is the low-frequency end of visible light.

## Two theoretical spectra

```{julia}
#| echo: false
freqs = range(0.001, 0.5; length=400)
ar1_spectrum(f, a) = 1 / (1 - 2a * cos(2π * f) + a^2)

fig = Figure(; size=(900, 330))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1];
    xlabel=L"\text{frequency } f",
    ylabel=L"S(f)",
    yscale=log10,
    title="theory, not simulation",
)
lines!(
    ax,
    collect(freqs),
    fill(1.0, length(freqs));
    linewidth=3,
    color=:black,
    label=L"\text{white noise}",
)
for (i, a) in enumerate([0.5, 0.9])
    lines!(
        ax,
        collect(freqs),
        [ar1_spectrum(f, a) for f in freqs];
        linewidth=3,
        color=colors[i],
        label=L"\text{AR(1)}, a = %$(a)",
    )
end
axislegend(ax; position=:rt)
fig
```

# Some examples

## Five test signals

```{julia}
#| output: false
n = 20_000

white_noise = randn(n)
ar1 = simulate_ar([0.7], n)
ar2 = simulate_ar([1.2, -0.7], n)
seasonal = [sin(2π * t / 12) + 0.5 * randn() for t in 1:n]

function lorenz_x(n; dt=0.01, subsample=10)
    total = n * subsample
    x, y, z = zeros(total), zeros(total), zeros(total)
    x[1], y[1], z[1] = 1.0, 1.0, 1.0
    for i in 1:(total - 1)
        x[i + 1] = x[i] + dt * 10.0 * (y[i] - x[i])
        y[i + 1] = y[i] + dt * (x[i] * (28.0 - z[i]) - y[i])
        z[i + 1] = z[i] + dt * (x[i] * y[i] - (8 / 3) * z[i])
    end
    return x[1:subsample:end]
end

lorenz = lorenz_x(n)
```

The Lorenz system from Monday is included as a deterministic comparison (no noise term).

## What they look like

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
series = [
    ("white noise", white_noise),
    ("AR(1), a = 0.7", ar1),
    ("AR(2), 1.2 and -0.7", ar2),
    ("period 12 plus noise", seasonal),
    ("Lorenz x", lorenz),
]

function each_panel(f; size_px=(950, 400), axis_kwargs...)
    fig = Figure(; size=size_px)
    for (i, (name, x)) in enumerate(series)
        ax = Axis(fig[(i - 1) ÷ 3 + 1, (i - 1) % 3 + 1]; title=name, axis_kwargs...)
        f(ax, x, i)
    end
    return fig
end
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
each_panel() do ax, x, i
    lines!(ax, x[1:150]; linewidth=1.0, color=colors[i])
    hideydecorations!(ax)
    hidexdecorations!(ax)
end
```

```{julia}

    stem!(ax, collect(acf_lags), autocor(x, acf_lags); color=colors[i])

end
```

## Partial autocorrelation

```{julia}
#| echo: false
pacf_lags = 1:40
each_panel(; xlabel=L"\text{lag } h", ylabel=L"\hat\phi_h") do ax, x, i
    stem!(ax, collect(pacf_lags), pacf(x, pacf_lags); color=colors[i])
    hlines!(ax, [0]; color=:black, linewidth=0.8)
    ylims!(ax, -0.8, 1.05)
end
```

The Lorenz $x$ has alternating partial autocorrelations that decay slowly, unlike any finite-order AR model.

## Spectra

```{julia}
#| echo: false
each_panel(; yscale=log10, xlabel=L"\text{frequency}", ylabel=L"\text{power}") do ax, x, i
    pg = welch_pgram(x .- mean(x), 2048, 1024; fs=1.0)
    lines!(ax, freq(pg)[2:end], power(pg)[2:end]; linewidth=1.5, color=colors[i])
end
```

## Why the AR(2) peak is where it is

The AR(2) spectrum is $S(f) = \sigma^2 / |1 - a_1 e^{-2\pi i f} - a_2 e^{-4\pi i f}|^2$.

The denominator expands to

$$
|1 - a_1 e^{-2\pi i f} - a_2 e^{-4\pi i f}|^2 = (1 - a_1 \cos 2\pi f - a_2 \cos 4\pi f)^2 + (a_1 \sin 2\pi f + a_2 \sin 4\pi f)^2
$$

The peak sits at the frequency where this denominator is smallest.
Setting the derivative to zero and using $\cos 4\pi f = 2\cos^2 2\pi f - 1$:

$$
f_{\text{peak}} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\arccos\!\left(\frac{-a_1(1 - a_2)}{4a_2}\right)
$$

```{julia}
#| echo: false
a1_ar2, a2_ar2 = 1.2, -0.7
f_peak = acos(-a1_ar2 * (1 - a2_ar2) / (4 * a2_ar2)) / (2π)
period_peak = 1 / f_peak
@printf("f_peak = %.3g (period = %.3g time steps)", f_peak, period_peak)
```

## American River autocorrelation and spectrum

```{julia}
#| echo: false
river_lags = 0:730
pg_river = welch_pgram(centered, 8192, 4096; fs=1.0)
f_river = freq(pg_river)[2:end]
p_river = power(pg_river)[2:end]

a_river = autocor(log_flow, [1])[1]
white_level = var(centered) * 2
red_level = [
    white_level * (1 - a_river^2) / (1 - 2a_river * cos(2π * f) + a_river^2) for
    f in f_river
]

fig = Figure(; size=(950, 330))
ax1 = Axis(
    fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{lag (days)}", ylabel=L"\hat\rho_h", title="autocorrelation"
)
lines!(
    ax1, collect(river_lags), autocor(log_flow, river_lags); linewidth=1.5, color=colors[1]
)
hlines!(ax1, [0]; color=:black, linewidth=0.8)
ax2 = Axis(
    fig[1, 2];
    xlabel=L"\text{frequency (cycles per day)}",
    ylabel=L"\text{power}",
    xscale=log10,
    yscale=log10,
    title="spectrum",
    xticks=(
        [1 / (20 * 365.25), 1 / (5 * 365.25), 1 / 365.25, 1 / 30, 1 / 7],
        ["20 yr", "5 yr", "1 yr", "30 d", "7 d"],
    ),
    xticklabelrotation=π / 4,
)
lines!(ax2, f_river, p_river; linewidth=1.2, color=colors[1], label=L"\text{data}")
lines!(
    ax2,
    f_river,
    red_level;
    linewidth=2.5,
    color=:black,
    linestyle=:dash,
    label=L"\text{AR(1) fit}",
)
hlines!(
    ax2,
    [white_level];
    color=:gray,
    linestyle=:dot,
    linewidth=2,
    label=L"\text{white noise}",
)
axislegend(ax2; position=:lb)
fig
```

Both axes are logarithmic, the convention for a spectrum spanning decades of frequency and power.

Nothing stands above the red-noise fit at two to seven years, where the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) would sit.

## Spectrogram

A **spectrogram** computes a spectrum in each of several overlapping windows of $m$ points:

$$
S(f, t) = \left| \sum_{s=1}^{m} w_s\, x_{t+s}\, e^{-2\pi i f s} \right|^{2}
$$

The frequency resolution is $1/m$, so a longer window separates nearby frequencies but blurs their timing.

## American River spectrogram

```{julia}
#| echo: false
spec = spectrogram(centered, 1461, 730; fs=1.0)
spec_f = freq(spec)
keep = findall(f -> 1 / 800 < f < 1 / 60, spec_f)

fig = Figure(; size=(900, 330))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1];
    xlabel=L"\text{year}",
    ylabel=L"\text{period (days)}",
    yscale=log10,
    yticks=([60, 91, 182, 365, 730], ["60", "91", "182", "365", "730"]),
)
hm = heatmap!(
    ax,
    1915 .+ time(spec) ./ 365.25,
    1 ./ spec_f[keep],
    log10.(power(spec)[keep, :])';
    colormap=:viridis,
)
hlines!(ax, [365.25]; color=:white, linestyle=:dash, linewidth=2)
Colorbar(fig[1, 2], hm; label=L"\log_{10} \text{power}")
fig
```

The frequency grid is linear in $f$ but the $y$-axis is $\log$ period, so long periods get coarser blocks.

## The half-year band fades

```{julia}
#| echo: false
river.year = year.(river.date)
river.doy = dayofyear.(river.date)

function mean_cycle(mask)
    return [mean(flow[mask .& (river.doy .== d)]) for d in 1:365]
end

early = mean_cycle(river.year .<= 1955)
late = mean_cycle(river.year .>= 1965)

fig = Figure(; size=(900, 330))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1];
    xlabel=L"\text{day of year}",
    ylabel=L"\text{mean flow (cfs)}",
    title="the average year, before and after",
)
lines!(ax, 1:365, early; linewidth=2.5, color=colors[1], label=L"1915-1955")
lines!(ax, 1:365, late; linewidth=2.5, color=colors[2], label=L"1965-2015")
axislegend(ax; position=:rt)
fig
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
function harmonic_amplitudes(cycle)
    days = collect(1:365)
    y = cycle .- mean(cycle)
    first_harmonic = hypot(sum(y .* cos.(2π * days / 365)), sum(y .* sin.(2π * days / 365)))
    second_harmonic = hypot(
        sum(y .* cos.(4π * days / 365)), sum(y .* sin.(4π * days / 365))
    )
    return second_harmonic / first_harmonic
end

@printf(
    "1915-1955: peak on day %d, second harmonic is %.2f of the first\n",
    argmax(early),
    harmonic_amplitudes(early)
)
@printf(
    "1965-2015: peak on day %d, second harmonic is %.2f of the first",
    argmax(late),
    harmonic_amplitudes(late)
)
```

## Friday

Lab 2 runs a two-variable model of ENSO with fixed parameters and no trend, then samples 50-year windows from it.
